items.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to block lower court ruling keeping protected status in place for Venezuelan nationals
items.summary:
The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelans from going into effect. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

items.title: Where Lawyers Got The Word ‘Boilerplate’
items.summary:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day! 

Lawyers churn out “boilerplate” every day — the standard, reusable clauses tucked at the end of every contract. But the word has a surprisingly industrial, pre-legal origin, and it didn’t start in a law office at all. Where did “boilerplate” come from? 

Hint: It passed through the newspaper business before it ever reached the law, and the very first “boiler plates” were exactly that: made of steel.

items.title: Work-Life Integration For Lawyers Who Want Their Time Back
items.summary:
When I started my coaching business in 2004, I had networking meetings in the morning, more of them at night, and a desk covered in business cards from people I was supposed to follow up with. Most weekends were already spoken for by family commitments. Today, I rarely work nights or weekends, and I can take a morning or an afternoon off without feeling like the whole business will come to a screeching halt. If you’d told me back then that I could have that kind of flexibility, I would’ve asked what the hell you were talking about. Today I’d call it work-life integration.

So, what is work-life integration for lawyers? Where work-life balance can sound like giving work and home equal time every day, work-life integration is about making those commitments fit together over the course of a real week. You might put in a late night before a filing and still be able to take Friday afternoon off. The trouble starts when every night turns into a late night and Friday afternoon is the first thing you give up. The real challenge here is in finding efficiencies that allow you to achieve your goals without adding to your already jam-packed schedule. 

Here are three changes that helped me get some control back and that I now work on with lawyers.

Become A Student Of Time Management 

When I started my business, I had stacks of paper on my desk, stacks of business cards from people I needed to follow up with and enough unopened emails that finding the one I actually needed felt like a project. At one point, my assistant and I gathered all the loose paperwork into a single pile. It…

items.title: Can You Legally Ditch Work And Family Chores To Play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ In Peace?
items.summary:
In less than 24 hours, “Grand Theft Auto VI” will be available to play. As one of the most anticipated games ever, there is speculation that its release will negatively affect workplace productivity and divert spending away from other forms of entertainment, including bars and amusement parks.

Rockstar in its infinite wisdom opted to release the game at midnight local time on a work night. Most people will either wait until the next day to play or play the game for a few minutes after midnight before going to bed.

But the true GTA fans will grab their espresso, Red Bull, or their energy drink of choice and play until they crash out at 4 a.m. While some had the foresight to request time off from their job, others did not and will have to choose between going to work half-asleep or not show up to work and explain why to their boss.

Most people will attempt to binge-play the game for hours or even days with no interruptions. To head off family discord, some fans have drafted tongue-in-cheek “leave me alone” contracts. For a set period, the player is exempt from chores and relatives agree to refrain from interruptions or snide remarks.

For employees wanting time off to play the game, planning could help a lot.

Only a few states require giving employees paid time off (PTO) or paid vacation. Employers generally offer PTOs as a fringe benefit. Since PTOs can be used for any reason, including playing a video game, an employee does not have to disclose why he or she is using it. But in most cases, an employee must give their employer adequate notice and the employer must…
items.t: Can You Legally Ditch Work And Family Chores To Play ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ In Peace?

items.title: That Didn’t Take Long: The First Biglaw Firm To Match Cravath!
items.summary:
It’s a match! Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton has answered Cravath’s long-awaited compensation move within a day. The firm is matching the new salary scale, the year-end bonuses, and the over-the-top special bonuses. Cleary is one of the usual suspects for an early match each bonus season, so the speed isn’t a shock.

On bonuses, Cleary took Cravath’s numbers line for line. Year-end bonuses run from $15,000 (prorated) to $115,000. Special bonuses run from $11,000 (prorated) to $40,000, well above the $6,000 to $25,000 Milbank paid this summer . Like Cravath, Cleary has no billable-hour requirement. Per the memo, “The Firm does not apply any billable-hour requirement in determining eligibility for the year-end bonus and the special bonus.”

Bonuses will be paid December 18, and associates have to be “actively employed by the Firm and in good standing” that day. The new salaries take effect January 1, 2027, and will show up in the January 15 payroll.

There’s one Cleary quirk, as always. The memo says the salary figures “include the Firm’s contribution to associates’ TOPS accounts.” As we’ve explained before , TOPS is the firm’s contribution to associates’ 401k accounts: rather than paying all of that money out directly, Cleary puts a set percentage of what would otherwise be salary toward retirement.

items.title: No, Supreme Court Gun Case Isn’t Based On A ‘Misquote.’ What Scalia Did Was Way More Intellectually Dishonest
items.summary:
Last week, The New York Times reported that the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment case law rests upon a “misquote.” In Heller , Justice Scalia assembled a string cite of some armchair history, asserting that tradition only recognized restrictions on firearms that are both “dangerous and unusual.” Since then, judges have copied and pasted that language to strike down all manner of gun laws. But, the Times argued, Scalia’s language misquotes the cited source. The quoted language appears before a cite to William Blackstone, even though Blackstone wrote that weapons may be regulated if they are “dangerous or unusual.”

Irate conservatives spent the week blasting the Times for not understanding how signals work. See, Scalia began that cite with the “See” signal, they remind us! That means he obviously wasn’t directly quoting the phrase he chose to place in quotation marks for some reason. Jonathan Adler opened his Volokh Conspiracy response to the controversy with “This is stunning.” Cam Edwards at Bearing Arms went with “journalistic malpractice.” Stunning! Malpractice!

And, yes, the signal does mean that Scalia wasn’t attributing the direct quote to the sources that follow. “See” doesn’t promise the source uses the same words. That said, “See” does suggest the following work supports the proposition and, in this case, it absolutely does not .

Here’s what Scalia wrote:

We think that limitation is fairly supported by the historical tradition of prohibiting the carrying of “dangerous and unusual weapons.” See 4 Blackstone 148–149 (1769); 3 B. Wilson, Works of the Honourable…

items.title: Xi, Putin, Trump, And Musk Assemble In China To Decide How To Divide Up The World Among Them
items.summary:
Who is the richest man in the world? Ask Google’s crappy AI this question, and it will give you a clear-cut answer: Elon Musk, now worth a bit less than the trillion-dollar mark which his fortune had previously summited.

Yet, Musk might only be definitively seen as the world’s richest man because his wealth is relatively easy to measure. All you have to do is look at what shares of Tesla and SpaceX are trading at, determine what his stake is in these companies, and do some simple multiplication.

Many forms of wealth are not so easy to measure. It’s certainly valuable to be able to whisper the name of one of your critics to a trusted lieutenant, and be assured not only that that person will suddenly fly off of a hotel balcony or succumb to an exotic poison but also that you will face no consequences whatsoever for it.

Rich though he may be, Musk does not have that kind of power. Vladimir Putin does, though.

Now, if you’re thinking that I’m conflating wealth with power, you’d be correct. Like space and time are different expressions of the same fundamental material, wealth is a means of exerting power — of getting people to do what you want.

Russia’s nominal GDP is close to $3 trillion. If at any time for any reason Putin wants to put any part of that economy to use, to build himself another mansion or to hire more bodyguards to pick up his poop while he’s abroad or to pay for a war to try to steal a neighboring country, all he has to do is reach out and take it (and he has). While it may be hard to put a dollar net worth to Putin, by measure of what he is capable of…

items.title: In-House And AI: You Can’t Demand What You Don’t Understand
items.summary:
It’s a mystery. Most in-house counsel want their outside firms to aggressively use AI, and most expect their bills to be reduced. Yet, they rarely demand these things from their outside firms. It’s a counterintuitive gap. What gives?

A recent Axiom study sheds some light. Put simply, a lot of in-house counsel don’t have any more of a clue how to use AI effectively than do their outside firms. If the people paying the bills don’t understand what AI can realistically accomplish, how can they know what to demand? How can they hold the people sending the bills accountable?

The Study and Its Source 

Now we do need to start with a little healthy skepticism. Axiom is an alternative legal service provider (ALSP). Its primary mission is to supply in-house legal departments with legal talent for specific and often temporary needs. So it’s in Axiom’s interest if in-house legal needs help with AI. That does not necessarily mean the survey results are wrong. I have no evidence of that. But it’s always good to keep in mind who is paying for work like this.

Axiom sponsored the study and commissioned InsightDynamo , which describes itself on its website as a healthcare research firm (Hmm …). InsightDynamo surveyed 528 in-house legal professionals online at companies with annual revenues of at least $100 million. The survey was done between March 13, 2026, and March 25, 2026.

A Lack Of Metrics, Skills, And Use 

The results paint a bleak picture of in-house legal’s understanding and effective use of AI. Of those surveyed, 83% don’t know how to measure AI’s ROI or assess how their…
items.t: In-House And AI: You Can’t Demand What You Don’t Understand

items.title: The Supreme Court before it stood apart
items.summary:
The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press)

***

In her excellent new book,  The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History , professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “ umpire ,” is not nearly as  originalist  as we tend to assume.

Shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different;…
items.t: The Supreme Court before it stood apart

items.title: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket
items.summary:
The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024 . The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “ is at any time found ” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years . As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years .

The state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It…
items.t: An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

items.title: Where The ‘Cravath Scale’ Actually Began
items.summary:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day! 

For generations, every Biglaw associate’s paycheck was measured against the “Cravath scale,” the lockstep benchmark that top firms race to match. It all traces to a single raise in 1968, when Cravath, Swaine & Moore “blew the ceiling off” the market by jumping its first-year starting salary to a then-shocking new figure, sending Wall Street firms scrambling to keep up. What was that 1968 starting salary, the number that launched the modern associate pay wars? 

Hint: Rival firms grudgingly matched it, then raised billable-hour targets and lengthened the partner track to afford it. Adjusted for inflation, that 1968 figure is worth roughly $145,000 today, well under the $235,000 base a Cravath first-year starts at now. 

See the answer on the next page.

items.title: ALERT: Cravath Makes Its Associate Compensation Move!
items.summary:
Well, there it is.

It’s finally happening! On Tuesday, Cravath announced its year-end bonuses, its special bonuses, and a new associate salary scale, all in one memo. That’s the same Cravath that has spent the better part of half a year letting the rest of Biglaw stew in its silence .

The new base salaries start at $235,000 for the class of 2026 and go up to $440,000 for the class of 2020. That matches the scale Milbank set when it kicked off the 2026 salary wars on June 2 . But Cravath’s new salaries take effect January 1, 2027, while Milbank’s took effect July 1.

Back in August, we floated the theory that Cravath might hold everything until bonus season. That way it could announce year-end bonuses, match Milbank’s specials, and unveil the new salary scale all at once, and get the last word.

Well. That’s exactly what happened.

items.title: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?
items.summary:
(Photo by CRASH:candy/Flickr) 

AI is rearing its head in our courtrooms, and judges are having to decide what to make of it. Two recent decisions show a wrong way and a right way to do just that.

I recently wrote about a federal district court judge in Texas, Mark Pittman, who excoriated some attorneys because he thought they used AI to draft briefs. And because he didn’t like the arguments that they made. He labeled the lawyers lazy and called their arguments tortured. All before holding a hearing. It was my view that this was the wrong way to look at AI and those who use it. 

Then along came an opinion out of the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky. To me, it represents the right and studied way for courts to view AI and its use. The judge there denied a motion to dismiss by a cop who allegedly relied on AI facial recognition, and only AI, to make an arrest. 

The cases are factually different. One involved lawyers using AI, the other a cop. But both turn on the same question: how should a court think about AI and its use by those appearing before it?

The Alleged Kentucky Facts 

A Black man entered a bank in Florence, Ky., and attempted to cash what appeared to be a fraudulent check. The bank refused to cash the check, and he left. A security camera captured an unobstructed view of his face. 

A local police department detective named Kilmer allegedly took a screenshot of the man’s face from the footage. He then used AI facial recognition technology to match that screenshot with a booking photo on file. The cop took the booking photo and a…
items.t: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?

items.title: Where Should AI Expertise Live In Legal?
items.summary:
Getty Images 

Curt McDaniel and I have been talking about Legal Operations for a long time, and not just theoretically.

Before retiring in 2025, Curt spent 19 years at Ferring Pharmaceuticals, including six as Chief Legal Officer, where he led a significant evolution in how the global legal function delivered its services. Curt and I have spent years looking at Legal Operations from opposite sides of the table.  

Over the years, we’ve stayed in touch, and Curt and I still regularly compare notes about where the profession is headed. Not surprisingly, lately those conversations have included a lot of artificial intelligence “what-ifs.”

We agree on a lot, including that AI needs to be part of a broader legal strategy, not a standalone technology project.

But one question has generated more debate between us than most:

Where should AI expertise actually live inside Legal? 

My perspective is that Legal Ops may have to become the AI expert inside the legal department. As AI’s capabilities have evolved, so has Curt’s view. He sees a need for deep AI expertise in an in-house legal team, led by Legal Ops and supported by lawyers with some level of expertise.

Our discussion led us to ask: What kind of AI expertise does Legal Operations truly need? 

Legal Ops Shouldn’t Become IT 

Curt raises an important concern: AI isn’t a Legal-only technology. It cuts across the entire enterprise, and organizations already have teams responsible for technology, data, security, privacy, finance, and other areas critical to implementing it responsibly.

Legal can’t simply build its own AI…
items.t: Where Should AI Expertise Live In Legal?

items.title: Death By A Thousand Cuts: Breaking An Already Broken Immigration System
items.summary:
Describing just how dysfunctional the U.S. immigration system has gotten is becoming increasingly difficult.

The headlines tell one story: immigrants detained, families separated, businesses reconsidering visa sponsorship, or being suspended from sponsoring altogether, and ever-changing policies creating widespread uncertainty.

But behind those headlines lies a much larger, largely invisible crisis: the immigration system itself is breaking down.

When people learn that I am an immigration attorney, they often say, “Wow, you must be busy!”

Yes, immigration lawyers are incredibly busy. But not necessarily doing the work we should be doing. Instead of helping employers recruit talent, and families reunite, we spend an extraordinary amount of time correcting government errors, troubleshooting dysfunctional filing systems, and navigating bureaucratic chaos.

We are busy doing busywork. 

And the consequences are far from trivial. Every administrative failure creates uncertainty, delays, additional costs, and sometimes life-altering consequences for the people and businesses depending on the system.

Here is what that looks like in practice.

1. Getting An Application Accepted Has Become An Obstacle Course 

In my 20 years practicing immigration law, simply getting an application accepted for filing has never been this difficult.

Applications are rejected over filing fees, payment processing, and technicalities, even when we follow published instructions.

The United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) frequently attributes payment failures to banks…

items.title: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once
items.summary:
On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

***

Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a) . According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado .

Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal…
items.t: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

items.title: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently
items.summary:
Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy , on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy 

Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free…
items.t: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

items.title: Listening to the past
items.summary:
Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded , but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

The role of history in text-and-history cases 

Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary…
items.t: Listening to the past

items.title: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket
items.summary:
Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “ So Ordered .” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”

Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

The volume fell, but not to normal 

In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

For most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump…
items.t: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers.

items.title: Ecuadorian fishermen who survived US boat strikes sue Trump administration
items.summary:
US military has killed nearly 250 people in attack on ‘narco-terrorism’, and on 17 March, sank the 16 plaintiffs’ boat, leaving two with serious burns

More than a dozen Ecuadorian fishermen are suing the US government after they survived a military drone attack in the Pacific ocean earlier this year that sank their boat and left two of them with serious burns from the explosions.

The 17 March attack on the La Negra Francesca Duarte II was part of the Trump administration’s Operation Southern Spear campaign, announced in November 2025 ostensibly to counter “narco-terrorists” it said operated in the Caribbean and Pacific.
